book.title: When: The Scientific Secrets of Perfect Timing
book.author: Daniel H. Pink

confidence_note: Duke anesthesia figures come from a published excerpt of When and the Duke press release; Danish test and nap details from reader highlights and reviews; no full text available. Hand-washing is from Pink's interviews and left out of the story. Old claims (2-4 p.m. accident share, NASA/Google/Japan nap policies, 'five minutes and coffee') are not verified and were dropped. Hand-washing and vigilance time-outs come from Pink's interviews and a book summary (medium).
facts: Pink cites a Duke study of about 90,000 surgeries: anesthesia problems were significantly more frequent for cases starting in the 3 and 4 p.m. hours, about 1% at 9 a.m. versus 4.2% at 4 p.m.
Actual patient harm was 0.3% at 8 a.m. and 1% at 3 p.m.; the researchers said afternoon circadian lows impair doctors' vigilance.
Danish schoolchildren scored worse on tests taken later in the day; a 20 to 30 minute break 'to eat, play, and chat' before the test raised scores, and the gain was larger than the hourly decline.
Pink's 'nappuccino': drink coffee, then nap; caffeine takes about twenty-five minutes to enter the bloodstream.
Ideal naps run ten to twenty minutes; longer brings sleep inertia. Five-minute naps did little; ten-minute naps had effects lasting nearly three hours.

Pink's comparison for the Danish break: the boost was like students having about three extra weeks in the classroom; and 'if there were a break after every hour, test scores would actually improve over the course of the day.'
Pink's rules for a restorative break: moving beats stationary, social beats solo, outside beats inside.
Duke researchers also noted most anesthesia events were not serious harm.
Pink cites University of Pennsylvania research showing hand-washing in hospitals deteriorates considerably in the afternoon.
The Duke authors also pointed to end-of-day fatigue and afternoon hand-offs between staff.
Pink describes hospitals adding 'vigilance' time-outs, short structured breaks, to counter afternoon errors.
scene_details: Danish children breaking to eat, play and chat
tension: Same hospital, same anesthesiologists, yet the 4 p.m. case is about four times riskier than the 9 a.m. case.
opening_idea: Open on the operating schedule: a surgery booked for 4 p.m.

lessons.idea: Plan a short real break before anything that needs care in the afternoon, instead of pushing through the trough.
lessons.example: An accountant who files reports after lunch takes a quick walk outside before checking the figures.

reflect_final: What careful task usually lands in your mid-afternoon, and what short break could you put right before it?

use_cases.situation: Booking an important appointment or procedure.
use_cases.move: Ask for a morning slot and mention the Duke anesthesia data Pink cites.

use_cases.situation: Team review always set for 3 p.m.
use_cases.move: Propose a fifteen-minute break before it, like the Danish test break.

use_cases.situation: Partner fading every afternoon on weekends.
use_cases.move: Suggest a coffee followed by a twenty-minute nap and see how the evening goes.

pocket_idea: Coffee, then a nap under twenty minutes: the caffeine arrives as you wake.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: At one hospital, anesthesia problems were about four times as frequent at 4 p.m. as at 9 a.m.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Pink: at Duke, afternoon operations had far more anesthesia problems; Danish kids tested worse later but a 20-30 minute break erased the drop; his fix is the nappuccino, coffee then a short nap.
conversation_variants.question_idea: When does your afternoon slump hit?
